chunks: "The three I'd name are UART, SPI and I2C. All of them are serial, so a byte goes out one bit at a time. UART is the simplest.
It's two wires plus ground, TX and RX, and it's point to point. There's no clock.

Both sides agree on a baud rate ahead of time, the line idles high, a start bit pulls it low to wake the receiver, then you send the data bits, least significant first, and a stop bit puts it back high.
The receiver samples in the middle of each bit using its own clock. SPI is synchronous.
The controller drives a clock, SCLK, and sends data out on MOSI while the device sends data back on MISO at the same time, so it's full duplex.
Each device has its own chip-select line, and you pull it low to talk to that device. It's fast, tens of MHz is normal, but you pay one pin per extra device.
I2C uses just two wires, clock and data, shared by every device.
Each device has a 7-bit address, the controller sends a start condition, the address, and a read or write bit, the addressed device acknowledges, then data bytes follow, each acknowledged.
The lines are open-drain with pull-up resistors, so it's slower, typically 100 or 400 kilohertz, but you can hang lots of devices on two pins."
